title: From Market Women to Female Professionals: Can Artificial Intelligence Transform Women's Economic Lives in Ghana?
text_paragraph_1: Artificial intelligence is gradually changing how people conduct business, perform their professional duties and earn a living. What once appeared to be a technological development reserved for advanced economies is increasingly becoming part of everyday life in Ghana. From banking and education to healthcare, agriculture and trading, digital technologies are opening new possibilities for economic growth. Yet, an important question deserves attention. Can artificial intelligence genuinely improve the economic lives of Ghanaian women, particularly those whose livelihoods depend on small businesses, informal trading and professional employment?
text_paragraph_2: This question is especially relevant because women occupy an important place in Ghana's economy. Walk through Makola Market in Accra, Kejetia in Kumasi or any major trading centre across the country, and one cannot overlook the determination of women who sustain businesses, support families and contribute to local economic activity. Beyond the markets, women serve as teachers, nurses, bankers, administrators, entrepreneurs and professionals in many other fields. Their daily contributions demonstrate that women's economic advancement is inseparable from Ghana's broader development.
text_paragraph_3: However, many of these women continue to work under difficult conditions. Limited access to affordable credit, inadequate business information, rising operating costs, unequal employment opportunities and competing family responsibilities often restrict their economic progress. Artificial intelligence may not resolve all these challenges, but its responsible application could provide practical opportunities for improving productivity, expanding businesses and strengthening women's financial independence.

text_paragraph_2: Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, and unpredictable seasons. Heat stress, flooded cities, loss of biodiversity and drought. The list of climate change’s adverse effects on the African continent is long. While locally experienced, the repercussions travel through social networks and mobility practices, intensifying already changing dynamics in and between rural and urban areas.
text_paragraph_3: This policy brief examines the implications of living with climate change in Somaliland and Ghana, based on 29 interviews with policymakers, experts, activists and civil society organisations in Hargeisa in 2025 and Accra in 2026. Despite significant ecological, political and economic differences between these two contexts, both sets of interviews highlight climate change as upending rural livelihoods and accelerating already rapid urbanisation, tendencies also found elsewhere on the continent. 1

According to them, this assistance is provided to young Congolese, even though both communities attend the same classrooms and live in similar conditions. They decry this disparity in treatment and are calling on the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to intervene to ensure fair access to humanitarian aid.
text_paragraph_2: Burundian refugees state that their youth do not receive the same assistance as their Congolese peers, particularly regarding school supplies. They argue that basic needs should not be assessed based on nationality, especially when pupils share the same desks and follow the same curriculum.
text_paragraph_3: “When there is a lack of school supplies, it’s a problem for everyone! Imagine giving notebooks to two Congolese children while leaving out a Burundian child, even though they sit at the same desk. This is an injustice committed by United Nations agencies,” laments a Burundian refugee.

title: Rumonge : schools accused of pressuring underage pupils to register for the 2027 presidential election
text_paragraph_1: Rumonge, November 2, 2026 — Officials from several secondary schools in the port town of Rumonge, in Burunga province, southwestern Burundi, are accused of pressuring pupils to register to vote in the 2027 presidential election. According to local sources, some pupils were taken to registration offices, while classes were reportedly suspended at some schools to allow them to gather the required documents.
text_paragraph_2: The operation took place from Monday, October 26, to Wednesday, October 28. It reportedly targeted pupils born in 2008 and 2009, some of whom were under 18 at the time of registration.
text_paragraph_3: According to local sources, in some schools, national identity card numbers were reportedly given to pupils without the corresponding cards being issued to them beforehand. These numbers allegedly allowed them to register to vote without presenting the physical documents.

Des patients atteints de cette maladie ont été transférés à l’hôpital Roi Khaled et à l’hôpital Prince Louis Rwagasore. Les autorités ont également confirmé des cas dans la zone de Gihosha, ravivant les inquiétudes face aux risques de propagation.
text_paragraph_2: À l’hôpital Roi Khaled, un patient hospitalisé pour une autre maladie se dit préoccupé par l’arrivée régulière de personnes atteintes de choléra dans cet établissement.
text_paragraph_3: « La situation est inquiétante. Depuis la semaine dernière, ils ne cessent de recevoir des patients atteints de choléra. Il n’y a pas un jour sans qu’un nouveau malade soit signalé », témoigne-t-il.

title: Burundi : overcrowded prisons, hunger, and lack of care worsen the poverty of inmates
text_paragraph_1: Bujumbura, November 4, 2026 — Prison conditions remain alarming in Burundian prisons. In its report covering the period from July to September 2026, the Action of Christians for the Abolition of Torture (ACAT-Burundi) denounces critical prison overcrowding, food shortages, deaths related to health problems, and cases of prolonged detention despite court-ordered release.
text_paragraph_2: According to statistics from the Burundian League for Human Rights, Iteka League, cited in the report, the country’s prisons held 12,521 inmates at the end of September 2026, while their capacity was only 4,294. The occupancy rate thus reached nearly 292%, almost three times the intended capacity.
text_paragraph_3: The situation is particularly worrying in several facilities. Mpimba Central Prison in Bujumbura, Burundi’s commercial capital, held 4,226 inmates in a facility designed for 800. In Muramvya, in the center of the country, 771 inmates were recorded in a facility with a capacity of 100. In Ngozi, in the north, the men’s prison held 1,889 inmates in a facility designed for 400. The prison in Gitega, the political capital, held 1,450 inmates in a facility designed for 400.

His eldest son, Teodoro Nguema Obiang , serves as the country's vice president and has become internationally notorious for his lavish lifestyle, expensive real estate purchases, and involvement in multiple foreign money-laundering investigations.
text_paragraph_3: Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo was born on June 5, 1942, in Akoakam-Esangui, a village in what was then Spanish Guinea. He grew up in the Mongomo district, near the border with Gabon, and belonged to the Fang ethnic group. He attended local schools and received part of his early education through Catholic missionary institutions.

title: Migration and human security in eastern Senegal: moving beyond the security lens
text_paragraph_1: In Goudiry, in the Tambacounda region, the migration issue is especially acute, at the crossroads of economic fragility, social dynamics and security concerns. On 29 October 2026, the Timbuktu Institute, in partnership with the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, held a meeting there to present the findings of its study “Migration, Resilience and Human Security”, which focuses on the departments of Goudiry and Bakel. Bringing together local elected officials, the prefect, civil society representatives, young people, returning migrants and the defence and security forces (DSF), the meeting opened up for discussion the central conviction that migration cannot be reduced to a question of security or crime. Rather, it must also be understood through its economic and social dimensions, in particular its role in community resilience mechanisms.
text_paragraph_2: The validation workshop forms part of a broader reflection on the links between migration, economic resilience and human security in eastern Senegal. Located in the Tambacounda region, some 650 kilometres from Dakar, the departments of Goudiry and Bakel are among the oldest migration basins in West Africa. They are also on the front line of the repercussions of the security crisis affecting Mali’s Kayes region, just across the border. In these territories, human mobility, cross-border solidarity and economic vulnerability are closely intertwined, in ways that security-only frameworks do not always capture. It was with this in mind that the Timbuktu Institute and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation organised this workshop, opened by Dr Bakary Sambe, Regional Director of the Timbuktu Institute, and Marie Nguettia, Programme Officer, in the presence of Alséyni Bangoura, Prefect of the department. Representing the Regional Director of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, Dr Armin Osmanovic, the Foundation’s representative recalled the aim of the exercise: to test the study’s conclusions against the realities experienced by local stakeholders, in order to arrive at a final document that takes into account the aspirations and recommendations of local communities.

text_paragraph_1: October brings another significant stage of UK employment reform. Changes under the Employment Rights Act include longer time limits for employment tribunal claims, with the general limit increasing from three to six months from 1 October 2026, alongside further reforms relating to trade unions and harassment. Employers also have more change on the horizon: the government is progressing its plans on dismissal and re-engagement and enhanced protection for pregnant women and new mothers , while a major consultation is considering employment status reform and protections for the self-employed , with responses due by 8 January 2027. A separate government review is examining potential whistleblowing reform , including mandatory workplace policies and possible financial rewards.
text_paragraph_2: Italy has adopted a legislative decree to align its framework with the EU AI Act : employers may not rely solely on AI systems for key decisions such as hiring, dismissals, disciplinary action and performance evaluations and workers must receive clear information about AI systems used. Implementation of the Gender Pay Transparency Directive continues, with the latest Dutch bill making hirers, rather than staffing agencies or other lenders, responsible for reporting on the pay of agency workers. Family protections are expanding too: from 1 October 2026, Finnish employers must automatically give written reasons when a protected employee’s fixed-term employment ends or is not renewed , while Spain has introduced new rights for employees with care responsibilities and new protected sick leave categories for certain menopause-related conditions .
text_paragraph_3: Employers in China that engage workers beyond retirement age should review their arrangements following the Interim Provisions on the Protection of the Basic Rights and Interests of Over-Age Workers , which took effect on 1 July 2026. Although over-age workers are not employees under PRC labour law, they now have core statutory protections that cannot be contracted out of. Overtime limits and overtime pay rates under the PRC Labour Law now apply, and employers must enrol over-age workers in work-related injury insurance and pay the premiums. text_paragraph_1: Bank of Botswana chose steadiness over surprise on Wednesday, leaving its main interest rate untouched for another cycle even as inflation retreated from the uncomfortable heights it reached in late summer. The decision, delivered after a meeting of the Bank of Botswana’s Monetary Policy Committee, keeps the Monetary Policy Rate anchored at 5.5 percent and signals that policymakers are prepared to wait out a stubborn price surge rather than choke off a fragile recovery.
text_paragraph_2: The committee, chaired by Governor Lesego C. Moseki, voted unanimously to hold the line. In doing so, it threaded a familiar needle confronting monetary authorities the world over: how to keep borrowing costs high enough to tame inflation without snuffing out the first real growth the economy has seen in two years.
text_paragraph_3: The headline number offered a measure of relief. Consumer price inflation eased to 7.8 percent in September, down sharply from 9.3 percent a month earlier. But the decline flattered to deceive. Much of it reflected a statistical quirk, the fading “base effect” of a fuel-price jump recorded in September 2025 that had, on its own, padded the inflation rate by nearly a full percentage point.

During his presidency, Equatorial Guinea transformed from an impoverished former Spanish colony into a major oil and natural gas producer, generating billions of dollars in petroleum revenues. However, the country's newfound wealth has been accompanied by widespread allegations of government corruption, political repression, and the concentration of economic resources within the president's family. His eldest son, Teodoro Nguema Obiang , serves as the country's vice president and has become internationally notorious for his lavish lifestyle, expensive real estate purchases, and involvement in multiple foreign money-laundering investigations.
text_paragraph_3: Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo was born on June 5, 1942, in Akoakam-Esangui, a village in what was then Spanish Guinea. He attended local schools and received part of his early education through Catholic missionary institutions.

How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
text_paragraph_1: “It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.” The El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas — including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa — and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.
text_paragraph_2: Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.
text_paragraph_3: Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”

text_paragraph_1: November 6, 2026, appears to have marked half a year without a U.S. strike on the Islamic State in Somalia.
